title: tui2: tool call labels never show arguments, only tool name
description:
internal/tui2/tools.go renderTool and renderToolBox build their label as t.name, special-cased ONLY for the skill tool (skillLabelFromArgs extracts the skill name from args). Every other tool - shell included - shows only the bare name, both while running and after completion. The '- summary' suffix visible for grep/edit/read is the RESULT content (t.result), not the call arguments, so a shell call in particular gives the user zero visibility into what command is executing or executed until they dig into chat history separately.

WebUI's ToolCard.vue already does this correctly: displayLabel is always tool.argumentsSummary, shown live from call start. This is a TUI/WebUI drift (see tau-architecture-principles) and a safety gap - the operator cannot see a risky shell command before or while it runs, only the tool name.

Confirmed not caused by feat/agent-tool-efficiency: that branch never touches internal/tui2/tools.go.
acceptance_criteria: A running or completed shell/grep/read/edit/write/find tool call shows a one-line preview of its actual arguments (e.g. the shell command, the grep pattern, the file path) in both the collapsed list row and the box title, not just the tool name. Unknown/plugin tool names and malformed argument JSON fall back to the bare name unchanged. Existing skill-label behavior is unchanged.
close_reason: Generalized toolArgLabel from the skill-only special case to shell/grep/read/edit/write/find, used at both renderTool and renderToolBox label sites so it applies while running (not just after completion). Closes the TUI/WebUI drift with ToolCard.vue's displayLabel. Pushed as fix/tui2-tool-arg-visibility off main.

title: Fix ambiguous provider routing in model picker
description: Model IDs can be advertised by multiple enabled providers. Preserve the selected provider/model pair through model-picker selection so Tau routes requests through the provider shown on the selected row.
acceptance_criteria: Selecting a duplicate model ID uses the provider shown in the chosen row in both TUI frontends; tests cover duplicate IDs.
close_reason: Preserved provider-qualified identity through both TUI model pickers and added duplicate-ID regression coverage.

title: coordinator: alias common tool-name mistakes and list real tools on unknown tool
description: 'unknown tool' occurred 10 times across the corpus, including the literal names bash, shell, skill and agent, plus 6 malformed calls. coordinator_turn.go:557 and :570 return a bare 'unknown tool: X'. Map well-known aliases (bash->shell etc) to the real tool, and when a name is genuinely unknown include the list of available tool names so the model can self-correct in one turn.
acceptance_criteria: A call to an aliased name executes the real tool; a genuinely unknown name returns an error listing available tools; existing unknown-tool tests still pass.

title: read: return a directory listing instead of erroring on a directory path
description: 'path is a directory, not a file' occurred 10 times (read.go:105). The model's intent is always clear in this case. Return the directory listing so the turn continues instead of burning a round trip on an error.
acceptance_criteria: read on a directory returns a listing, not an error; listing is bounded; read-before-write tracking is NOT marked for directories.

title: edit: report nearest match on stale_edit instead of a generic 'must match exactly'
description: stale_edit accounts for 11 of 163 edit calls (6.7%). editNotFoundError (internal/agent/tools/edit.go:283) only says the text must match exactly, including whitespace and indentation, which forces a full re-read of the file to recover. Locate the closest match in the file and return its actual current text with line numbers so the retry succeeds without a re-read.
acceptance_criteria: A near-miss old_text produces an error naming the line number and showing the actual current text; an old_text with no plausible match still produces the generic error; no edits are written on failure.

title: read/grep/find: allow read-only access to GOMODCACHE instead of erroring
description: sandbox_escape is the single largest avoidable error class: 18 occurrences (grep 13, read 4, find 1), all Go module cache lookups. read.go:98 and grep.go:127 already return a hint telling the model to use shell with 'go env GOMODCACHE', and the model still repeatedly hits the error, so the hint is not working. Allow the read-only tools (read, grep, find) to resolve paths under GOMODCACHE while keeping the mutating tools (edit, write) strictly confined to the workspace.
acceptance_criteria: read/grep/find succeed on paths under GOMODCACHE; edit/write still reject them; paths outside both workspace and GOMODCACHE still rejected.

title: read: skip re-sending unchanged, already-served line ranges
description: Top 30 repeated-read groups account for 279 calls and 236,367 tokens = 23.6% of all tool result tokens. internal/agent/coordinator.go was read 58 times in one session (43% line overlap); internal/tui2/model.go appears 4 separate times in the top 30. ~54k tokens (5.4% of total) are literally the same lines re-sent. ReadTracker (internal/agent/tools/read_tracker.go) already records path->bool for the read-before-write check; extend it to record file identity (size+mtime+hash) and the line ranges already served, and have read.go return only novel lines when a re-read overlaps an already-served range of an unchanged file.
acceptance_criteria: Re-reading an unchanged file over an already-served range returns a short notice instead of the body; changed files always return full content; read-before-write tracking still works.

title: grep: clamp context lines and give grep its own byte cap
description: Worst single tool result in the corpus was 12,811 tokens: grep with context_before=2, context_after=10, limit=80 over internal/providers/snapshot/models.json. Three of the top ten token outliers are grep-with-context over that same JSON file. grepDefaultLimit is 100 but the byte cap is the shared DefaultMaxBytes = 50KB (internal/agent/tools/truncate.go:11), which is enormous next to a 74-token median grep. Clamp context_before/context_after to a sane maximum and give grep a dedicated, smaller output cap.
acceptance_criteria: context_before/context_after are clamped with a visible notice; grep output capped well below 50KB; normal small greps are unaffected.
notes: Byte cap half already landed in 8b8d5b0 (2026-07-11): grepMaxBytes=24KB plus grepMaxLineChars=500 line truncation, both applied in capGrepResult on the ripgrep and fallback paths. The 12,811-token outlier in the report predates that commit. Remaining scope is the context_before/context_after clamp, which is still unbounded: 10 lines of context across 100 matches spends the whole 24KB cap on padding rather than distinct matches.

title: Epic: agent tool-loop efficiency (tokens, success rate, latency)
description: Analysis of 77 tau sessions (1904 tool calls, ~1.0M result tokens, 105 errors / 5.5%) found read=58.5% and grep=29.0% of all tool result tokens, with a heavy tail: 27% of reads and 13% of greps carry ~two thirds of their tool's tokens. This epic tracks the fixes for token waste, avoidable tool errors, and shell latency.
acceptance_criteria: All child issues closed; task check green.
close_reason: All 11 child issues implemented, tested and verified end to end against the real repo; task check green.

title: Add structural parity guards for custom YAML config decoders
description: Config and nested config types use hand-maintained raw shadow structs in UnmarshalYAML to support aliases and duration parsing. A prior real regression silently discarded Metrics because rawConfig omitted the field; current tests protect that named incident but do not ensure future exported YAML fields are represented by the decoder. The same drift risk exists in AgentsConfig and other manual decoders.
design: Reduce shadow duplication where practical by decoding through alias/inline structures plus explicit legacy aliases. Add reflection- or fixture-based structural parity tests that fail whenever an exported YAML field is added without decoder handling and prove snake_case/camelCase precedence and zero/false semantics.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Adding an exported YAML field to Config or a manually decoded nested type without mapping it makes a test fail. 2. All current fields round-trip from representative non-zero YAML values without silent loss. 3. Canonical snake_case, supported camelCase aliases, explicit false/zero values, and duration errors have defined tests. 4. The decoder implementation has a documented single update point for new fields.

title: Keep plugin manager locks out of plugin process and RPC calls
description: Plugin Manager.Load holds the write lock while starting processes and calling metadata/capability/docs/tools RPCs. DispatchEvent, RunExtensionCommand, and reload result collection hold a read lock across plugin RPCs, while Unload holds the write lock while closing views and killing processes. A slow or malicious plugin can therefore block unrelated commands, reload/unload, and manager reads for full timeout chains; event dispatch is also sequential across plugins.
design: Separate registry state synchronization from external calls. Snapshot generation-bound client handles under lock, release the lock for process/RPC work, and commit or retire state safely with lifecycle/generation checks so reload cannot race a stale call into the new registry. Consider bounded parallel event dispatch while preserving deterministic response merge order.
acceptance_criteria: 1. No manager mutex is held while starting/killing a process, invoking host callbacks, or making plugin RPCs. 2. Reload/unload safely retires a generation without corrupting tools, docs, commands, capabilities, or views. 3. A hanging plugin does not prevent reads or another plugin from receiving an event beyond its own timeout. 4. Response merge order remains deterministic. 5. Race-enabled tests cover dispatch versus reload/unload, startup failure, timeout, and stale-generation completion.
notes: Fixed in PR #180 (git.catlow.cloud/sam/tau): https://git.catlow.cloud/sam/tau/pulls/180. Assumption recorded: Load/Unload racing each other is treated as a rare defensive case (normal use is single ReloadExtensions caller sequentially); a Load that loses the CAS race reports an error and retires rather than retrying to converge.
close_reason: PR #180 opened: replaced RWMutex-guarded maps with atomically-swapped registrySnapshot; reads never block on manager lock, Unload/Load never hold a lock during process spawn/kill or plugin RPCs, DispatchEvent parallelized with deterministic merge order. All ACs covered by new race-enabled tests; task check green.

title: Centralize root and child agent instantiation semantics
description: internal/agent/instantiate.go is the root instantiation implementation, while internal/agent/tools/agent.go explicitly mirrors its config, model resolution, depth enforcement, capability attenuation, spec snapshot, persistence, and collision retry to avoid an import cycle. internal/agent/tools/child_prompt.go likewise mirrors root prompt data and template behavior. These copies govern security-sensitive effective-tool attenuation and can drift independently.
design: Extract dependency-neutral instantiation and prompt-rendering primitives into a leaf package importable by both agent and tools. Keep caller-specific concerns at the edges: root trust-gate resolution remains pre-resolved by the root caller, and child session ID/seeding remains owned by the child caller. Preserve nil-as-unrestricted tool semantics explicitly.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Root and child paths use one implementation for model resolution, depth caps, effective-tool intersection, snapshot/hash construction, and instance-ID collision retry. 2. Root and child spec-body rendering share one template data contract and func map. 3. Mirrored structs/functions and comments are removed. 4. Table tests prove root/child parity, nil/unrestricted attenuation, spawn narrowing, depth limits, collisions, and template variables. 5. Existing agent-process tests and repository quality gates pass.
close_reason: Extracted shared instantiation/prompt-rendering into internal/agent/instance and internal/agent/prompttmpl; mirrored code removed; parity/depth/collision/nil-attenuation tests added; task check passes. Pushed as refactor/tau-3gq-centralize-agent-instantiation, PR not yet opened.

title: Harden plugin installation paths, integrity, and atomic replacement
description: Plugin IDs/names flow into filepath.Join for install, uninstall, and direct GitHub install with incomplete validation; the direct parser only rejects '/'. Direct GitHub assets are downloaded and executed without checksum/signature verification, downloads are unbounded, and replacement renames from an OS temp directory before chmod, which can fail across filesystems or leave an unusable replacement. The installer pipeline currently has no tests.
design: Introduce one validated plugin identifier/path resolver used by registry and direct installs plus uninstall/status operations. Stage bounded downloads inside the destination filesystem, verify an explicit trusted digest or documented release checksum policy before activation, set executable permissions before atomic replacement where supported, and preserve/restore the prior binary on failure. Make HTTP/filesystem dependencies testable.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Empty, dot, dot-dot, absolute, separator-containing, volume-qualified, and platform-specific escape names cannot resolve outside pluginsDir. 2. Downloads enforce a configurable size limit and reject integrity mismatches before activation. 3. Failed download, verification, chmod, or replacement leaves the prior installed plugin intact. 4. Same-filesystem atomic replacement works on supported platforms with explicit Windows behavior. 5. Table/integration tests cover registry and GitHub sources, traversal attempts, oversized payloads, checksum failure, and rollback.
notes: Fixed in PR #181 (git.catlow.cloud/sam/tau): https://git.catlow.cloud/sam/tau/pulls/181. Assumption recorded: no CLI flag/registry field carries an explicit trusted digest for direct GitHub installs, so the checksum-policy AC is satisfied by honoring a goreleaser-style checksums manifest when published, and clearly warning (not silently trusting) when absent.
close_reason: PR #181 opened: single validated plugin-identifier/path resolver used everywhere a name touches the filesystem, bounded+staged-in-pluginsDir downloads, atomicReplace with backup/restore on failure, and GitHub checksums-manifest verification when published. All ACs covered by new install_test.go and extended plugin_source_test.go; task check green.

title: Fix child runtime event subscription and one-shot cancellation
description:
## Problem
internal/app/child.go sends StartChatSessionCommand, LoadSessionCommand, and SubmitChatPromptCommand before it subscribes to ChatEvent. The event bus only routes publications to subscribers registered at publish time, so a fast completion/error can be lost and the child can wait forever. The same loop selects from cancelCh after the channel is closed; because a closed channel remains ready, it repeatedly sends CancelChatRequestCommand and can starve terminal-event handling. Existing child tests stop at handshake/provider setup and do not exercise this lifecycle.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run RunChild with a deterministic coordinator/streamer that publishes a terminal event immediately after SubmitChatPromptCommand.
2. Observe that the child subscribes only after the submit and never receives that terminal event.
3. Close stdin or send agent.cancel.
4. Observe the select loop repeatedly taking the permanently-ready closed cancelCh and sending cancellation until a different case wins.
design: Create the child ChatEvent subscriber before the first coordinator command. Convert stdin cancellation into a one-shot state transition (for example nil the channel after the first receive) while continuing to wait for the authoritative cancelled/completed event. Exercise the real event bus and coordinator boundary with deterministic fakes rather than timing sleeps.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The child subscribes before any command can publish an event it must observe. 2. EOF or agent.cancel sends at most one CancelChatRequestCommand. 3. Fast completion, runtime error, and cancellation each produce exactly one agent.result and terminate. 4. Regression tests fail under the old ordering and closed-channel loop. 5. go test ./internal/app/... and the repository quality gate pass.

title: Emit cumulative child usage and count model iterations correctly
description:
## Problem
The wire contract defines agent.usage as cumulative totals emitted after every completed turn, and the parent reader/UI already handles it, but internal/app/child.go never writes agent.usage. Its final AgentResultUsage.Turns is incremented on ChatToolExecutionStartedEvent, which counts tool calls instead of model/agent-loop iterations. Token totals also only use LastUsage, so multi-iteration child work is under-reported.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run a child that completes directly without tools; inspect agent.result and observe turns is 0 rather than 1.
2. Run a child with multiple parallel tool calls in one model iteration; observe turns equals the number of tool starts rather than model iterations.
3. Run a multi-iteration child and inspect stdout; observe no agent.usage envelopes and final tokens limited to LastUsage.
design: Make coordinator iteration/usage totals available through an authoritative event or completion payload, then have the child emit cumulative agent.usage updates and use the same totals in agent.result. Do not infer turns from presentation events. Keep one definition for cumulative semantics across child writer, bridge types, parent accumulator, and UI state.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A no-tool completion reports one model iteration. 2. Multiple parallel tool calls in one iteration do not increase the turn count. 3. Multi-iteration runs emit monotonic agent.usage messages with cumulative input/output tokens and cost. 4. agent.result carries the same final cumulative totals. 5. Protocol and child integration tests cover zero-tool, sequential-iteration, parallel-tool, cancellation, and budget-exhaustion cases.

title: Replace minio/selfupdate to close unfixable openpgp advisory (GO-2026-5932)
description: govulncheck flags GO-2026-5932 (golang.org/x/crypto/openpgp unmaintained/unsafe) in the root module via github.com/minio/selfupdate. No fixed version exists. The package is unreachable today (internal/updater verifies updates via SHA-256 checksum, never calling selfupdate's openpgp signature APIs), so the advisory was accepted and documented during remediation (commits c5e048e/56703e1). Long-term fix: replace minio/selfupdate (unmaintained since ~2023) with a maintained binary-swap mechanism, or vendor the needed atomic-replace + rollback logic.
acceptance_criteria: tau update no longer depends on golang.org/x/crypto/openpgp; govulncheck ./... reports zero findings at all levels

title: grep: engage the codesearch index for subdirectory searches
description: searchBackends across the corpus was {codesearch: 11, direct: 199} - the index served only 5% of searches. grep.go:133 only engages the index when filepath.Clean(searchPath) == filepath.Clean(cwd), so any search scoped to a subdirectory silently falls back to a full direct walk. Widen the condition to any path under cwd by filtering the index candidates by path prefix.
acceptance_criteria: A grep scoped to a subdirectory under cwd uses the codesearch backend with candidates filtered to that subtree; results match the direct backend; a path outside cwd still uses direct.

title: agent: stop advertising non-spawnable specs to the model
description: The agent tool has a 73.3% error rate (11 errors in 15 calls). Three are 'spec X is not spawnable (disable-model-invocation: true)' from agent.go:198 for the research and plan specs, which are rejected at call time yet still advertised to the model. Filter specs with DisableModelInvocation out of the agent tool schema so the model never sees them as options.
acceptance_criteria: Non-spawnable specs are absent from the agent tool schema; calling one by name still errors clearly; spawnable specs are unaffected.

title: Web UI store deleteSession optimistically removes session from list before server confirms, masking delete failures
description:
Location: internal/webui/src/stores/session.ts (deleteSession function at line ~280)

The deleteSession function in the Web UI Pinia store sends a DeleteSessionCommand to the backend AND immediately removes the session from the local  list:

  function deleteSession(id) {
    sessions.value = sessions.value.filter((s) => s.id !== id)
    return sendEnvelope(command('DeleteSessionCommand', { session_id: id }))
  }

If the server-side delete fails (DB error, the session doesn't exist, or a permissions issue), the server emits a ChatRuntimeErrorEvent. However, the session is already gone from the client-side list, so the user sees no trace of the failed deletion. The error notification may be shown, but the user can't verify whether the delete actually happened.

Compare with the tui2 implementation (internal/tui2/commands.go line ~771) which does NOT optimistically remove the session — it only sends the command and waits for the SessionDeletedEvent (handled in internal/tui2/events.go line ~254) to update the list.

Additionally, the Web UI's handleSlashCommand function for /session delete (in ChatInput.vue) also calls deleteSession which has the same optimistic behavior.

Why it matters: A user who deletes a session and sees it disappear from the list believes it was permanently removed. If the server delete actually failed, the session remains in the database and the user doesn't know to retry. This is a data-integrity UX bug.

Suggested approach: Remove the optimistic removal from deleteSession() in the store. Let the SessionDeletedEvent handler be the sole mechanism for updating the session list, matching the tui2 pattern. If optimistic feedback is desired, show a temporary 'deleting...' state instead of removing the entry.

title: Web UI SettingsDrawer provider switch may produce invalid provider/model combinations
description:
Location: internal/webui/src/components/SettingsDrawer.vue (applyProvider function at line ~172)

When the user changes providers in the SettingsDrawer, the applyProvider function sends an UpdateChatSessionCommand with the new provider and the currently selected model ID:

  apply({ provider, model: { id: session.model } })

This hard-codes the current model ID into the patch, but that model may not be available on the new provider. Unlike the tui2, which has access to per-provider model lists and can verify compatibility, the Web UI blindly pairs the current model with the selected provider. If the model doesn't exist on the new provider, the next turn fails at the provider runtime level.

Additionally, the SettingsDrawer has no model selector — users must use the /model slash command to change models. There is no way to browse and select models from the settings panel.

Why it matters: Switching providers from the Web UI settings panel silently produces a broken provider/model combination. The error is only surfaced as a failed turn (ChatRuntimeErrorEvent) with no clear indication that the provider/model pair was invalid. The user must then guess which combination is valid.

Suggested approach:
1. In applyProvider, omit the model from the patch and let the backend's pickModel logic find a valid model on the new provider
2. Or add a model selector to the SettingsDrawer that shows only models available on the selected provider
3. At minimum, log a warning when the current model isn't found in the new provider's catalog

title: Web UI ChatInput completion menu offers commands that silently fall through to the model as prompts instead of being handled
description:
Location: internal/webui/src/components/ChatInput.vue (handleSlashCommand at line ~422)

The Web UI text input completion menu (triggered by typing /) offers completions for commands like /login, /logout, /provider, /reasoning, and displays extension commands. However, the handleSlashCommand() switch statement only handles: /model, /system, /effort, /new, /clear, /reset, /resume, /session, /reload, /refresh, /help, and /?. All other commands (including /login, /logout, /provider, /reasoning, /temperature, /max-tokens, and all extension commands like /mcp) return false from handleSlashCommand(), causing them to fall through to the submit() function which sends them as SubmitChatPromptCommand to the model.

The user sees these commands in the completion dropdown, selects them expecting command behavior, but the text gets sent to the LLM as a prompt instead.

Why it matters: This is misleading — the completion UI suggests functionality that doesn't exist. A user selecting /login from the dropdown will just send 'login' as a chat message to the model. It's both a UX bug and a regression from the tui2 where ALL commands are properly dispatched.

Suggested approach: Add handler cases for /provider, /login, /logout, /reasoning, /temperature, /max-tokens. For extension commands, route them to a RunExtensionCommandCommand. Make handleSlashCommand() return true only when it dispatched a real command, and false when unrecognized (current behavior). Add warnings for unrecognized commands.

title: Web UI store lacks handlers for ChildAgentMessageEvent, ExtensionCommandResultEvent, and several other bridge-emitted events
description:
Location: internal/webui/src/stores/session.ts (apply function)

The bridge in internal/bridge/wire.go registers and forwards 27 event types to WebSocket clients. The Web UI Pinia store's apply() function handles only 21 of them. The following events are forwarded by the bridge but silently discarded by the client:

1. ChildAgentMessageEvent — live child agent streaming updates don't render
2. ChildTranscriptLoadedEvent — child transcript loads don't populate the overlay
3. ExtensionCommandResultEvent — extension commands produce no visible output
4. ExtensionViewRenderedEvent — extension panels don't appear
5. ExtensionViewClosedEvent — extension panels don't get cleaned up
6. SessionExportedEvent — no export feedback

Why it matters: These are not future features — the backend already produces these events and the bridge already forwards them. The client silently drops them, so child agent transcript viewing, extension command output, and export feedback don't work in the Web UI. Users get no visible errors, just missing UI.

Suggested approach: Add handler cases for each event in the apply() function. For events that carry a message or path, call pushNotice(). For extension views, store the panel state. For child transcript events, maintain a transcript buffer.

title: Web UI store silently drops SessionExportedEvent, providing no user feedback on session export
description:
Location: internal/webui/src/stores/session.ts (apply function at line ~191)

The Web UI Pinia store's apply() function handles many ChatEvent types from the server but has no case for SessionExportedEvent. When a user exports a session via /session export, the backend emits a SessionExportedEvent with the output path, but the store silently discards it.

Compare with the tui2 handler (internal/tui2/events.go) which shows 'session exported: path'. The Web UI user sees no feedback at all after export — no success message, no path, no error.

Why it matters: The /session export command in the Web UI appears to do nothing. This is both a usability bug and a debugging obstacle.

title: isConfined does not resolve symlinks, allowing sandbox escape through project-internal symlinks
description:
Location: internal/agent/tools/pathutil.go — isConfined() function
Impacted tools: read.go, write.go, edit.go, find.go, grep.go (all use isConfined)

The isConfined function checks whether a resolved file path stays within the project working directory by comparing filepath.Rel(base, target) for ".." prefix escaping. However, it does NOT resolve symbolic links via filepath.EvalSymlinks before the comparison.

If a project directory contains a symlink pointing outside the project (e.g., /home/user/project/link -> /tmp/), a tool call with path "link/secret.txt" resolves via resolvePath to /home/user/project/link/secret.txt, passes isConfined (filepath.Rel returns "link/secret.txt", no ".." prefix), but os.ReadFile follows the symlink and reads /tmp/secret.txt.

This affects ALL file-accessing tools that use isConfined: read, write, edit, find, and grep. The indexing/codesearch.go package already handles this correctly via confinedWorkspaceFile which resolves symlinks with filepath.EvalSymlinks before path checking.

Why it matters: A cloned repository or third-party skill can contain a symlink pointing outside the workspace. When the model reads, edits, or searches files through that symlink path, it accesses files outside the intended sandbox. This defeats the confinement guarantee.

Suggested approach: Apply filepath.EvalSymlinks to both base and target before the filepath.Rel comparison in isConfined, matching the pattern used by confinedWorkspaceFile in internal/indexing/codesearch.go. Existing tests in tau-316 would cover this once the fix is applied.

title: Add conversation search across all sessions
description:
Location: internal/store/ (new search methods), internal/tui2/commands.go, internal/chat/types.go, internal/agent/coordinator.go

Currently there is no way to search the content of saved sessions from within tau. The /session command lists sessions but provides no text search across conversations. Adding a /search command that queries conversation text across all saved sessions would let users:

1. Find that conversation where they discussed a specific topic
2. Recall how they solved a particular problem
3. Locate a session by its content rather than its metadata

Suggested approach:
- Add an FTS5 virtual table to the SQLite schema (new migration) indexed on messages.content and messages.role
- Add ListSessionsCommand and ChatEvents for search results
- Add the /search command to both tui2 and legacy TUI command tables
- Surface results as a list of {session_id, snippet_with_matches, timestamp} entries
- Respect the existing pagination pattern used by List()

title: Add Markdown session export format
description:
Location: internal/store/ (new file), internal/agent/coordinator_persist.go, internal/chat/types.go

Currently the only session export format is JSONL (ExportSessionAsJSONL). Adding a Markdown export would let users:

1. Share conversations in a human-readable format without needing a JSONL-aware tool
2. Render sessions in markdown-aware viewers (Obsidian, GitHub, etc.)
3. Review session history outside tau for documentation or debugging

The Markdown export would render each message with role-based headers (## User, ## Assistant, ## Tool), display tool calls as fenced code blocks, show reasoning content in `<details>` blocks, and include session metadata (model, provider, token usage, cost, duration) as a YAML frontmatter block at the top.

Suggested implementation:
- Add a new function `ExportSessionAsMarkdown(ctx context.Context, store SessionStore, id string) (string, error)` in internal/store/ that reads messages via ExportMessages and formats them as Markdown
- Add a new `Format` field or type to ExportSessionCommand so users can choose format
- Support both file output and stdout

title: Add unit tests for the skill tool and tool-restriction functions
description:
## Location
`internal/agent/tools/skill.go` — `RegisterSkillTool()`, `ParseAllowedTools()`, `findSkill()`

## What's missing
The skill tool (`RegisterSkillTool`) is the LLM-facing mechanism for activating skills, which in turn can restrict the available tool set via `AllowedTools`. The `ParseAllowedTools` function parses the user-authored `allowed-tools` field from a skill's frontmatter into a concrete tool name list used by the coordinator's `SetAllowedTools`. Despite controlling what tools the model can invoke — a security-sensitive operation — none of these functions have unit tests.

The `findSkill` function does case-insensitive matching against the catalog and is called by both `RegisterSkillTool` (LLM-invoked) and `handleRunSkill` (slash-command-invoked). A regression here could cause name collisions to resolve incorrectly or valid names to not match.

## Why it matters
The skill tool is a privilege boundary: activating a skill with `allowed-tools` restricts the model's tool access. If `ParseAllowedTools` parses incorrectly (e.g., dropping valid tool names, or including names that shouldn't be there), the model gains or loses capabilities erroneously. If `findSkill` returns the wrong skill (e.g., two skills with near-identical names), the wrong tool restrictions apply.

## Suggested approach
Add table-driven tests for:
1. `ParseAllowedTools`: comma-separated, space-separated, mixed, empty input, leading/trailing whitespace, empty entries between commas, nil/empty result
2. `findSkill`: exact match, case-insensitive match, prefix mismatch, nil input, partial suffix match (should fail), empty skill slice, nil entries in slice
3. `RegisterSkillTool`: verify the tool is registered with correct name, schema, and executor (executor can be tested in isolation with a mock skillsMgr/tracker)

title: Add unit tests for security-critical path resolution and confinement functions
description:
## Location
`internal/agent/tools/pathutil.go` — `resolvePath()`, `isConfined()`
`internal/agent/tools/fsutil.go` — `writeFileAtomic()`

## What's missing
The `resolvePath` and `isConfined` functions are the sole gatekeepers for sandbox confinement — they prevent the LLM from reading or writing files outside the working directory. Every file tool (read, write, edit, find, grep) calls `isConfined` before operating and `resolvePath` to determine the absolute path. Despite this security-critical role, neither function has any unit tests.

Similarly, `writeFileAtomic` implements the atomic file replacement pattern used by the write and edit tools. It handles temp file creation, chmod, rename, and cleanup on error. No tests exist for its error handling paths (chmod failure, disk full, cross-filesystem rename, etc.).

## Why it matters
A regression in `isConfined` (e.g., a path normalization change that fails to detect `../` escape) would be a sandbox breakout vulnerability — the LLM could read or write arbitrary files outside the project directory. Without tests, the only defense against this is manual inspection of every change to these files.

A regression in `writeFileAtomic` (e.g., temp file leaking, rename failing leaving the old file in place) could silently lose data during file edits.

## Suggested approach
Add table-driven tests covering:
1. `resolvePath`: relative paths, absolute paths, `@`-prefixed paths, paths with `..`, paths with `.`, empty paths, symlink-containing paths (when relevant)
2. `isConfined`: paths inside base, paths outside via `..`, paths outside via unrelated absolute, empty base, base with trailing slash, same-file case, symlink resolution edge cases
3. `writeFileAtomic`: basic write, write to new dir, write to existing file, rename failure (cross-filesystem temp), chmod failure, cleanup on error

title: Bridge WebSocket lastSnapshot not updated on SessionLoadedEvent
description:
Location: internal/bridge/bridge.go — broadcastEvent() line

The bridge caches the most recent ChatSessionSnapshotEvent in b.lastSnapshot for replay to newly connecting WebSocket clients. The coordinator emits a SessionLoadedEvent (NOT a ChatSessionSnapshotEvent) when a session is loaded via /resume or /session load. Since the bridge only checks for ChatSessionSnapshotEvent in its cache logic:

```go
if _, ok := ev.(tauchat.ChatSessionSnapshotEvent); ok {
    b.mu.Lock()
    b.lastSnapshot = data
    b.mu.Unlock()
}
```

...the SessionLoadedEvent is never cached. A browser client connecting after a session load receives the OLD session snapshot, and renders the wrong conversation, model, and provider until the first subsequent turn produces a new ChatSessionSnapshotEvent.

Why it matters: Users of the Web UI who reload the page after resuming a different session see the old session until they submit a prompt. For sessions with no immediate follow-up prompt, the stale state persists indefinitely.

Suggested approach: Either (a) also check for SessionLoadedEvent in the broadcastEvent cache branch and cache its marshalled data under the lastSnapshot key, or (b) have the coordinator emit a ChatSessionSnapshotEvent alongside SessionLoadedEvent so the bridge catches it naturally. The first option is less invasive.

title: Tool loop breaker parseToolCallKey does not strip summary field from comparison key
description:
Location: internal/agent/coordinator_turn.go — parseToolCallKey() function

The parseToolCallKey function removes repeat_justification from the unmarshalled arguments before computing the comparison key, but does NOT remove the summary field (toolCallSummaryProperty = "summary") which is injected into every tool schema by injectSummarySchemaProperty(). The summary field is a model-authored one-liner describing what the call is doing, surfaced in the UI status bar while the tool runs.

Since summary can legitimately vary between calls (e.g. "Searching for error handler" vs "Looking for the cancel function") while the actual tool name and arguments remain identical, a model that happens to vary the summary field between calls will produce different comparison keys and evade the loop breaker entirely.

Why it matters: The loop breaker is a safety mechanism against degenerate tool-call loops. A model that varies the summary field can produce an unbounded sequence of identical tool calls without triggering either the soft threshold or the hard block limit. This was designed to prevent exact-repeat loops but the summary field creates a trivial bypass.

Suggested approach: Add `delete(m, toolCallSummaryProperty)` alongside the existing `delete(m, "repeat_justification")` in parseToolCallKey so summary is stripped from the comparison key like any other semantically-irrelevant field.

title: ExportSessionAsJSONL deadlocks with ExportMessages goroutine on file write error
description:
Location: internal/store/jsonl_export.go

When ExportSessionAsJSONL encounters a file write error (e.g. disk full, permission denied), it breaks from the for-range loop consuming ExportMessages() output, then attempts to drain any remaining messages via `for range ch {}`. Meanwhile, the ExportMessages goroutine continues sending messages to the buffered channel (capacity 64). If the goroutine has more than 64 remaining messages, the channel becomes full, the goroutine blocks on `select { case out <- line: case <-ctx.Done(): }` — but ctx is not cancelled because the consumer has no cancellation handle. The drain loop then blocks waiting for the channel to close, while the producer blocks waiting for the channel to be read. Result: permanent deadlock.

Why it matters: A simple export of a session with more than ~64 remaining messages after a write error permanently blocks the goroutine — the deadlock only resolves when the 30-second timeout from the caller (handleExportSession) fires. The export call returns an error (context deadline exceeded) rather than the actual write error, making debugging harder.

Suggested approach: Derive a separate cancellable context inside ExportSessionAsJSONL from the caller-provided ctx, and cancel it when the write error is detected so the ExportMessages goroutine can exit via its ctx.Done() path and close the output channel cleanly.

title: Edit, Read, Find, and Docs tools create timeout contexts that are never applied
description:
## Location
- `internal/agent/tools/edit.go:124` — `makeEditExecutor`
- `internal/agent/tools/read.go:92` — `makeReadExecutor` (two instances in fallback paths)
- `internal/agent/tools/find.go:79` — `makeFindExecutor`
- `internal/agent/tools/docs.go:66` — doc read sub-function

## What's wrong
All four of these tools use the following pattern to create a timeout context:

```go
_, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, DefaultToolTimeout)
defer cancel()
```

The returned context (first return value) is assigned to `_` (blank identifier) and discarded. The original `ctx` from the function parameter is used for all downstream I/O operations (file reads, command execution, etc.), so the timeout context has zero effect. The cancelled variables are only used for defer cleanup.

The same bug in `write.go` is tracked by tau-6wa ("Write tool discards timeout context, leaving file I/O unbounded"), but the edit, read, find, and docs tools have the identical pattern and are not covered by that ticket.

## Why it matters
Without an effective timeout, each of these tools can block indefinitely on:
- A slow or hung filesystem (NFS, FUSE mounts, network drives)
- A very large file read that takes longer than expected
- A blocked OS I/O call (pipe buffer full, cgroup I/O throttle)

The `DefaultToolTimeout` (60s) exists precisely to prevent these hangs, but is dead code in these tools.

## Suggested approach
Replace `_` with the new context variable (e.g., `readCtx`) and use it instead of `ctx` for all I/O operations within the executor. The `defer cancel()` pattern is already correct — only the assignment needs fixing.

title: Find tool POSIX -path argument does not sanitize user-supplied exclude pattern
description:
## Location
`internal/agent/tools/find.go:234` — `buildFindArgs()` function, POSIX find path

## What's wrong
The POSIX find branch of `buildFindArgs` constructs its exclude filter using:

```go
args = append(args, "-not", "-path", fmt.Sprintf("*/%s/*", p.Exclude))
```

The `p.Exclude` value comes directly from the model's tool call input (via JSON unmarshalling). It is embedded into a `-path` argument without any sanitization or escaping. A crafted exclude value containing spaces, wildcards, or find expression primitives (e.g., `-o`, `-prune`, `-name`) could change the structure of the find command.

Example problematic values:
- `foo -o -name bar` would be interpreted as `-not -path "*/foo -o -name bar/*"` which find treats as a literal path pattern, not an injection — find's `-path` is a single argument that glob-matches against the whole path. So this specific injection is actually limited by how find parses `-path`.

However, the constructed pattern `*/%s/*` wraps the user content in glob wildcards, meaning an exclude value of `*.go` becomes `*/*.go/*`, which would NOT match `foo/bar.go` as the user probably intended (intending to exclude all `.go` files, but the wrapping `*/.../*` requires it to be a directory component, not a leaf file).

The real issue: the fd branch correctly uses `--exclude` which is a dedicated predicate, but the POSIX fallback uses a poorly constructed `-path` glob that doesn't match the user's intent and has unusual semantics.

## Why it matters
Users who rely on the POSIX find fallback (no fd installed) get silently incorrect exclude behavior. The exclude pattern `*.go` would not match any files because the wrapping `*/.../*` expects the excluded name to be a full path component sandwiched between slashes.

## Suggested approach
For the POSIX find path, derive the exclude more carefully:
- Use `-not -name p.Exclude` for simple name-based excludes (most common case)
- For path-based excludes, use `-not -path "*/p.Exclude"` (one trailing wildcard, not wrapped) 
- Add a validation step that logs a warning when the exclude pattern contains characters that could interact with find's expression language

title: Coordinator turnCount never resets, permanently exhausting turn budget across sessions
description:
## Location
`internal/agent/coordinator.go:96` (turnCount field)
`internal/agent/coordinator_turn.go:68` (increment)
`internal/agent/coordinator_turn.go:1381` (check)

## What's wrong
The coordinator's `turnCount` field is initialized to zero in `NewCoordinator` and only ever incremented in `runTurn`. It is never reset to zero — not on session reset, not on session load, not on new session start, and not between turns. The guard in `checkLimits`:

```go
if c.maxTurns > 0 && c.turnCount > c.maxTurns {
    return "budget_exhausted", true
}
```

means that once the turn budget is exhausted, ALL subsequent turns (including brand new user submissions or loaded sessions) fail immediately. The only recovery path is restarting the coordinator.

While this primarily affects child agent instances where `maxTurns` is set (from spec snapshot limits), it also means the main interactive coordinator is one config change away from a hard-to-debug state where every prompt is silently blocked.

## Why it matters
A child agent that runs multiple task assignments on the same coordinator would fail permanently after the first task exhausts the budget. In the main coordinator, if `maxTurns` is ever set non-zero (e.g., via a config change), recovery requires a full tau restart.

## Suggested approach
Reset `turnCount` (and `cumulativeTokens`) at the start of each new turn in `handleSubmit`, or at least when a new session is loaded or created. This keeps the per-task budget semantics intact while preventing permanent coordinator-wide exhaustion.

title: Shell tool leaves orphan subprocesses on timeout/cancellation
description:
## Location
`internal/agent/tools/shell.go:makeShellExecutor` (and generally the shell tool path)

## What's wrong
The shell tool creates commands via `exec.CommandContext(ctx, shell, args...)` without calling `setProcessGroup(cmd)` first. When the context expires (timeout or cancellation), `exec.CommandContext` sends SIGKILL only to the immediate shell process. Any subprocesses spawned by the shell command (background tasks, build tools, server processes) survive as orphans.

The `setProcessGroup`/`signalProcessGroup` infrastructure already exists in `internal/agent/tools/procgroup_unix.go` and is used correctly by the agent spawning code (`internal/agent/tools/agent.go`), but the shell tool never calls it.

## Why it matters
A timed-out shell command can leave dangling subprocesses that consume resources, hold file locks, or continue modifying the filesystem long after the user thinks the command was stopped. Any make, npm run, cargo build, or shell pipeline that spawns children can orphan them.

## Suggested approach
Call `setProcessGroup(cmd)` before `cmd.Start()` in the shell executor. Override `cmd.Cancel` with a no-op (so the default Process.Kill() doesn't race with the process group kill) and add a cancellation goroutine that calls `signalProcessGroup(cmd, syscall.SIGKILL)` when the tool context expires or the tool is interrupted.

title: Auto-compact uses wrong model's context window to calculate token budget
Auto-export JSONL goroutine races with session store close on shutdown
description:
## Location
`internal/agent/coordinator_persist.go:293-300` — `persistSession()`

## What's wrong
When `autoExportJSONL` is enabled, `persistSession` launches an untracked goroutine for the JSONL export:

```go
if !c.autoExportJSONL {
    return
}
go func() {
    exportPath := c.sessionManager.SessionJSONLPath(state.SessionID, state.CreatedAt)
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := c.sessionManager.ExportToJSONL(ctx, state.SessionID, exportPath); err != nil {
        c.loggerWith(state.SessionID).Warn("auto-export jsonl failed", "err", err)
    }
}()
```

This goroutine is never tracked in any WaitGroup and is never waited upon. The coordinator's shutdown sequence is:

1. `Close()` → `c.cancel()`
2. `loop()` → `c.ctx.Done()` → `drainPendingCommands()` → `cancelAllSessions()` → which calls `persistSession` → launches goroutine
3. `loop()` exits → `<-c.loopDone` unblocks
4. `c.onClose()` runs (closes plugins, but NOT the session store)
5. `c.client.Close()` runs
6. `Close()` returns
7. Caller (`run.go:262`) closes `sessionManager`, which closes the underlying SQLite database

The goroutine from step 2 may still be running when step 7 closes the database, resulting in a "database is closed" error and a failed export.

## Why it matters
Auto-exported JSONL files are meant to be a reliable convenience artifact. A shutdown race silently drops them, and the only diagnostic is a logged warning. Users who rely on auto-exports to persist sessions across restarts lose data.

## Suggested approach
Track the export goroutine in the coordinator's `turnWG` (or a separate WaitGroup), and ensure it completes before the session store is closed. Alternatively, move the export call before the coordinator Close returns, or close the session store from within the coordinator's shutdown sequence.

title: Session list pagination drops rows when created_at timestamps collide
description:
## Location
`internal/store/sqlite_store.go:285-289` (`List` method)

## What's wrong
The `List` method uses a single-column `created_at` cursor for pagination:

```go
if cursor != "" {
    query += " WHERE s.created_at < ?"
}
query += " ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT ?"
```

When multiple sessions share the same `created_at` timestamp (e.g. sessions created in rapid succession, or at second-granularity resolution), the cursor condition `created_at < cursor` drops rows that have the same timestamp as the cursor row. The code itself acknowledges this in a NOTE comment:

```go
// NOTE: when multiple sessions share the same created_at, a
// composite (created_at, id) cursor would be more robust; the
// current single-column cursor may skip rows in that edge case.
```

## Why it matters
Users see an incomplete session list when multiple sessions were created within the same second. This is a data-loss bug during session browsing — sessions silently disappear from the list and can't be navigated to.

## Suggested approach
Use a composite `(created_at, id)` cursor as the comment suggests. Replace the single-column cursor with a two-column comparison, e.g. `WHERE (s.created_at, s.id) < (?, ?)`.

title: Write tool discards timeout context, leaving file I/O unbounded
description:
## Location
`internal/agent/tools/write.go:61-62`

## What's wrong
The write tool executor creates a context with timeout but discards the returned context:

```go
_, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, DefaultToolTimeout)
defer cancel()
```

The original `ctx` (not the timeout-derived one) is passed through to `writeFileAtomic`, `os.MkdirAll`, and `os.ReadFile`. None of these operations are bounded by the intended `DefaultToolTimeout`. The timeout and deferred cancel are effectively dead code.

## Why it matters
If a write hangs (e.g. NFS mount, slow disk, FIFO/special file), the tool executor blocks indefinitely. The coordinator's turn loop has no way to recover from a hung tool execution.

## Suggested approach
Pass the timeout-derived context to the downstream I/O operations. `writeFileAtomic` would also need to accept a context. Check whether edit and other file-mutation tools have the same pattern.
notes: Fixed in PR #184 (git.catlow.cloud/sam/tau): https://git.catlow.cloud/sam/tau/pulls/184. Scoped to write.go only per the ticket; edit/read/find/docs same-pattern bug is tracked separately as tau-dvy (not touched here to avoid overlap).

Verified regression test fails against pre-fix write.go and passes with the fix. task check green.

description:

title: Find tool POSIX fallback exclude pattern may skip user-supplied exclusion or match unintended files
description:
Location: internal/agent/tools/find.go — makeFindExecutor(), line ~287-288

The POSIX find fallback (used when the fd binary is not available) constructs the exclude filter as:

    if p.Exclude != "" {
        args = append(args, "-not", "-path", fmt.Sprintf("*/%s/*", p.Exclude))
    }

Two issues with this pattern:

1. The "*/%s/*" wrapper means the exclude pattern only matches PATHS CONTAINING the exclude value in an intermediate directory component, not the top-level directory itself. For example, an exclude of "node_modules" produces -path "*/node_modules/*". This correctly skips files inside node_modules/ at any depth. But the node_modules directory ITSELF would still appear in results (as an empty directory entry), though the subsequent "isDir" check typically filters it.

2. More importantly, when the exclude value CONTAINS GLOB METACHARACTERS (which are valid in user-supplied patterns like "*.test.*"), the pattern is interpolated directly into a -path argument with no escaping. For example, exclude="foo[bar]" becomes -path "*/foo[bar]/*". The POSIX find(1) interprets the brackets as a character class, not a literal. While this matches user intent for glob patterns, it could also match unexpected files if the pattern is crafted maliciously.

3. The most concrete functional issue: the exclude pattern is only wrapped as "*/%s/*" which means it does not exclude files that ARE the match at any level. E.g. exclude=".gitignore" becomes "*/.*gitignore/*" which only matches files INSIDE a .gitignore directory — but .gitignore is a file, not a directory. So excluding ".gitignore" doesn't work at all.

The fd-based exclude path (line 268-270) uses "--exclude" which handles all of these correctly because fd applies the glob intelligently (matches both files and directories at any depth).

Why it matters: Users relying on the POSIX find fallback (no fd installed) get unreliable exclude behavior. The pattern only excludes DIRECTORIES matching the pattern, not FILES, and only at intermediate directory depths.

Suggested approach: Use two -path patterns for the POSIX fallback:
    -not ( -path "*/exclude" -o -path "*/exclude/*" )
This excludes both the item itself and its contents at any depth. Better yet: detect fd availability at tool registration time and register the fd-based tool only when fd is available, falling back to a pure-Go filepath.WalkDir implementation instead of shelling out to POSIX find.

DiscoverContextFiles scans from filesystem root, potentially including unintended context files
description:
Location: internal/agent/prompt.go — DiscoverContextFiles() function

DiscoverContextFiles walks from the filesystem root (/) down to the project CWD, checking for AGENTS.md, .tau/AGENTS.md, .github/copilot-instructions.md, and .cursorrules at EVERY directory level along the path. For example, for a project at /home/user/projects/myapp, it checks:
  - /AGENTS.md
  - /.tau/AGENTS.md
  - /.github/copilot-instructions.md
  - /.cursorrules
  - /home/AGENTS.md
  - /home/.tau/AGENTS.md
  - /home/.github/copilot-instructions.md
  - /home/.cursorrules
  - /home/user/AGENTS.md
  - ... (and so on down to CWD)

While most of these won't exist, a .cursorrules or AGENTS.md placed in a home directory or system directory would be SILENTLY included in the system prompt without any indication to the user. This is not a vulnerability per se (the model already has full filesystem access through tools), but it means user home-directory configuration intended for a different tool could leak into tau's system prompt and affect agent behavior unexpectedly.

Why it matters: A user with a ~/.cursorrules (from Cursor editor) would have its entire contents injected into tau's system prompt without realizing it. The contents of these files may contain instructions that are incompatible with or irrelevant to tau's agent. There is no logging or notification that the file was picked up.

Suggested approach: Limit the walk to stop at the VCS root (git/hg) or at the user home directory, whichever is reached first currently. Also add a log line at Info level when a context file is discovered so users can audit what went into the prompt. Optionally add a tau config option to specify the context file discovery root directory.

title: Trust store Save uses non-atomic file write, risking corruption on crash
description:
Location: internal/trust/trust.go — Store.Save() method

The trust store Save method uses os.WriteFile() to write the YAML file directly:

    if err := os.WriteFile(s.path, data, 0o600); err != nil {

If the process crashes or loses power mid-write, the trust.yaml file contains partially-written YAML and becomes unparseable. The next Load() call returns a yaml.Unmarshal error, and the user sees a startup error rather than a cleared store.

Every other state-writing function in the codebase uses the atomic write pattern (create temp file in the same directory, write, fsync or close, rename over target):
- providers/state.go Save() uses CreateTemp + Rename
- store/sqlite_store.go transactions via SQLite WAL + atomic commit
- even writeFileAtomic in internal/agent/tools/fsutil.go uses temp+rename

Why it matters: A corrupted trust store means all trusted project root-spec overrides are lost on restart. The user must re-approve every project, which is a frustrating UX regression. Additionally, if the file is only partially written and Go yaml.Unmarshal returns an error, tau fails to load at all — the store has no recovery path to treat an unparseable file as empty.

Suggested approach: Replace os.WriteFile with the standard temp-file+rename pattern used by providers/state.go: create a .tmp file in the same directory, write the marshalled YAML, close it, then os.Rename over the target. Optionally add a fallback in Load(): if yaml.Unmarshal fails, log a warning and treat the file as empty (the trust entries are non-critical convenience state, not data).

title: Add config validation report command
description:
Location: internal/cli/ (new command), internal/config/config.go, internal/chat/types.go (new ConfigCheckCommand/ChatEvent)

The config package has a Validate() function that checks provider configurations, model_modes, agents settings, auto_compact, and metrics config. However, there is no way to run validation interactively or get a structured report of config issues. If tau starts with a misconfigured config.yaml, users only see the first validation error, not all issues.

A /config check or /config validate command would:

1. Run Validate() on the loaded config
2. Collect ALL validation errors (not just the first) into a human-readable report
3. Also check that:
   - Any model_modes entry references a configured provider
   - The default_provider actually exists in the providers list
   - Referenced environment variables for API keys are set (or empty but warned)
   - Plugin configurations have valid paths
4. Display the report as a formatted notification or system message

This is especially valuable for diagnosing config problems without restarting tau, and for users who inherit or modify config files by hand.

Suggested approach:
- Add a ValidateAll() function that collects all errors (not just the first) into a []error, then wraps them with context
- Add ConfigCheckCommand to chat/types.go
- Wire a handler in coordinator.go that runs ValidateAll on the current config and emits a notification with the full report
- Add the /config command to both TUI command tables
- Optionally add a tau config check CLI subcommand that prints the report to stdout

title: Add non-destructive conversation summarization command
description:
Location: internal/agent/coordinator.go (new command handler), internal/chat/types.go, internal/tui2/commands.go

The auto-compact feature destructively merges history (replaces old messages with a summary). There is no way to produce a summary of a conversation without modifying the session state. A /summarize command would:

1. Take the current conversation (optionally limited to the last N messages) and send it to the LLM for summarization
2. Display the summary as a ChatNotificationEvent or system message
3. NOT modify the session history — the summary is ephemeral or appended as a display-only message

This is useful for:
- Quickly recalling what was discussed in a long session
- Checking whether the model understood the context before submitting a prompt
- Getting a "tl;dr" of a child agent session from its transcript

Suggested approach:
- Add SummarizeSessionCommand and SummarizeSessionEvent to chat/types.go
- Wire a handler in coordinator.go that reads session messages, builds a compact prompt (reuse the compact agent spec), calls StreamChatCompletionFull with tools disabled, and emits a notification with the summary
- Add the /summarize command to both TUI command tables

title: Add unit tests for MutationQueue global lock serialization and cleanup behavior
description:
## Location
`internal/agent/tools/mutation.go` — `MutationQueue` struct, `GlobalLock()`, `GlobalUnlock()`, `Acquire()`, `Release()`

## What's missing
The `MutationQueue` serializes file mutations in two dimensions:
1. Per-file: concurrent edits to the same path are serialized via a per-file mutex entry
2. Global: shell commands acquire a global write lock that blocks all per-file mutations until the command completes

The existing tests (`mutation_test.go`, in external package) cover basic per-file serialization and different-path parallelism, but have significant gaps:
- No test for `GlobalLock`/`GlobalUnlock` (shell serialization against file mutations)
- No test for per-entry map cleanup after the last holder releases (to verify no memory leak)
- No test for the interaction between a held per-file lock and a concurrent `GlobalLock` (should block)
- No test for `GlobalLock` blocking new per-file `Acquire` calls
- No race detector validation of the RWMutex ordering

## Why it matters
The `MutationQueue` deadlock or memory-leak behaviors are subtle:
- If the per-entry cleanup doesn't remove the entry from the map when holders reach 0, the map grows unboundedly
- If `GlobalLock` doesn't properly block new `Acquire` calls (via the RWMutex read lock), a shell command races with concurrent file edits
- A deadlock between a holder of a per-file lock trying to global-lock and a global-lock holder trying to per-file-lock would stall all file operations

These are the kinds of concurrency bugs that only get caught by dedicated tests with the race detector enabled.

## Suggested approach
Add tests covering:
1. `GlobalLock` blocks new `Acquire` and unblocks after `GlobalUnlock`
2. `GlobalLock` waits for in-flight `Acquire` holders to release before proceeding
3. Per-entry map cleanup: acquire then release N times for M different paths, verify internal map is empty (via exported stats or direct inspection if exported)
4. Concurrent `Acquire` + `GlobalLock` with race detector: prove the lock ordering prevents deadlock
5. Many paths + one concurrent release per path — verify no entry remains after all releases

title: Add session tree visualization to Web UI
description:
Location: internal/webui/src/components/SessionSwitcher.vue, internal/webui/src/stores/session.ts

The session system has a parent-child hierarchy (sessions.parent_session_id, agent_instances.parent_instance_id) that enables agent spawning trees. The tui2 TUI has a /session-tree command and a dedicated overlay (sessiontree.go) for visualizing this hierarchy. The Web UI SessionSwitcher only shows a flat list of sessions with no parent-child relationship indicators.

Adding a tree visualization would let Web UI users:
1. See which sessions were spawned as child agents by other sessions
2. Navigate the agent spawning hierarchy visually
3. Understand the relationship between a research agent session and the parent conversation that spawned it

Suggested approach:
- Add a ListChildren endpoint to the WebSocket protocol (or use the existing SessionsListedEvent with parent info)
- Create a recursive tree component in Vue that renders indented child sessions under their parents
- Add expand/collapse interaction for tree nodes
- Show spec_name (agent identity) for each node alongside session metadata

title: Add unit tests for ReadTracker (read-before-write enforcement)
description:
## Location
`internal/agent/tools/read_tracker.go` — `ReadTracker` struct, `MarkRead()`, `CheckRead()`

## What's missing
The `ReadTracker` enforces the read-before-write safety invariant: the model must read a file before it can write or edit it. This prevents accidental overwrites of files the model hasn't inspected. Despite being the sole enforcement mechanism for this security property, it has zero unit test coverage.

The implementation uses a `map[string]bool` with a `sync.Mutex` for thread safety. Key behaviors that should be tested:
1. An unread file causes `CheckRead` to return an error
2. After `MarkRead`, `CheckRead` succeeds for the same path
3. Case sensitivity / path normalization (does `./foo` and `foo` resolve to the same recorded path?)
4. Thread safety under concurrent `MarkRead`/`CheckRead` calls (the race detector should pass)
5. Error message format (it includes the relative path for display)
6. Empty file paths

## Why it matters
A regression in the ReadTracker (e.g., path normalization that fails, or a mutex deadlock) would either:
- Block every write/edit because a read is never properly recorded (usability failure), or
- Allow writes to files the model hasn't read (defeats the safety guarantee)

Without tests, neither direction of regression is caught except by integration-style manual testing.

## Suggested approach
Add table-driven tests covering:
1. Reading a file then checking it — expect success
2. Checking a file before reading it — expect error
3. Path normalization: `MarkRead(cwd, "./foo")` then `CheckRead(cwd, "foo")` — expect success
4. Concurrent safety: race detector test with parallel MarkRead and CheckRead calls
5. Same file via relative and absolute paths — the path normalization should produce the same absolute key
6. Empty path and nil ReadTracker (tools handle nil rt gracefully)

title: Add unit test coverage for skills.go parsing, validation, and filtering functions
description:
## Location
`internal/skills/skills.go` — `SplitFrontmatter`, `UnmarshalFrontmatter`, `quoteColonValues`, `validateSkill`, `FilterDisabled`, `FilterUserInvocable`, `shouldReplaceSkill`, `shouldSkipDir`, `ToPromptIndex`, `ToPromptXML`, `escapeXML`, `bundledResourcesHint`, `AdditionalSources`, `cloneSkill`, `cloneSkills`

## What's missing
The skills package contains 20+ public and private functions for parsing YAML frontmatter, validating skill metadata, filtering/precedence, and rendering prompt XML, but has only a single test (`TestValidateSkill_LongInstructions`) that covers one validation rule.

Functions that handle user-authored YAML (`quoteColonValues`, `UnmarshalFrontmatter`) have zero test coverage despite being error-recovery paths that could produce incorrect results. The precedence logic (`shouldReplaceSkill`), filtering (`FilterDisabled`, `FilterUserInvocable`), discovery walking (`shouldSkipDir`), and prompt rendering (`ToPromptIndex`, `ToPromptXML`) also lack coverage.

## Why it matters
Skills are user-authored files that load at startup. A regression in parsing, validation, or precedence filtering produces incorrect skill activation — either a valid skill is silently ignored or an invalid skill produces a confusing error. Without tests, the only defense against regressions is manual testing.

## Suggested approach
Add table-driven tests for:
1. `SplitFrontmatter`: valid frontmatter, missing delimiters, unclosed delimiters, BOM prefix, CRLF line endings, empty content, no frontmatter
2. `UnmarshalFrontmatter`: valid YAML, colon-heavy values, already-quoted values, metadata section, folded `>` block scalars with URLs, literal `|` scalars
3. `validateSkill`: missing name, missing description, name too long, name with wrong characters, name/directory mismatch, instructions too long, compatibility too long
4. `FilterDisabled`/`FilterUserInvocable`: empty input, nil entries, disabled by name, enabled but disabled-by-field, mixed states
5. `shouldReplaceSkill`: priority ordering, same-priority tiebreak, case-insensitive matching
6. `ToPromptIndex`/`ToPromptXML`: empty set, populated set, bundled resources hint, DisableModelInvocation filtering, XML escaping

title: computeSpawnDeadline silently ignores malformed budget timeout, queue deadline is silently omitted
description:
Location: internal/agent/tools/spawn_admission.go — computeSpawnDeadline() function
Location: internal/agent/tools/agent.go — spawnChildProcess() function (920-990, budget validation block)

computeSpawnDeadline silently ignores malformed budget.timeout and budget.deadline fields by swallowing parse errors:

```go
if args.Budget.Timeout != "" {
    if d, err := time.ParseDuration(args.Budget.Timeout); err == nil {  // error swallowed
        consider(now.Add(d))
    }
}
```

The comment says "Malformed budget fields are ignored here — theyre validated and rejected properly once the spawn is admitted and reaches spawnChildProcess budget construction." However, by this point the child process has already been spawned (command.Start() at ~line 527), the handshake has completed, and budget fields are only validated in the budget-construction section of spawnChildProcess (~line 920-990, AFTER the handshake). If the timeout is malformed:

1. acquireSpawnSlot uses computeSpawnDeadline with no queue deadline → no queue timeout enforcement
2. The child process is started and the handshake succeeds
3. Only then does spawnChildProcess validate and reject the budget
4. The process is killed with SIGKILL, requiring wait/reap

Why it matters: A malformed budget.timeout (e.g. typo "5mm") causes a wasted child process spawn: it starts, handshakes, then is immediately killed when the budget validation rejects it. The queue timeout that was supposed to protect the spawn admission is silently omitted. While not a data-loss bug, it wastes resources and makes debugging harder (the error "invalid budget.timeout" arrives after the process has already started.

Suggested approach: Parse budget fields in computeSpawnDeadline AND report parse errors so the spawn is cleanly rejected at admission time rather than after the process starts. Alternatively, move the budget validation to run before cmd.Start().

title: Add test coverage for ExportSessionAsJSONL error and edge-case paths
description:
Location: internal/store/jsonl_export.go

The ExportSessionAsJSONL function has zero unit test coverage. The following code paths are untested:

1. File write error mid-export (disk full, permission denied) — the path that can deadlock (tau-3x3)
2. Session not found (ExportMessages sends error on errCh before any lines)
3. Context cancellation during message streaming (ctx.Done() path in the ExportMessages goroutine)
4. Empty session (zero messages — should produce an empty .jsonl file)
5. Temp file creation failure (os.Create failure)
6. Rename failure (os.Rename across filesystems)
7. The drain-loop after write-error path (for range ch after break)

Why it matters: The export path is used by both the auto-export-on-shutdown goroutine (coordinator_persist.go) and the /export command. Without tests, the deadlock in path (1) went undetected, and other production failures would silently corrupt or lose export output.

Suggested approach: Table-driven tests with injectable filesystem errors (via an interface or test helpers for os.Create/os.Rename/os.Remove). Cover each error path above plus the success path for sessions with 0, 1, and many messages.

title: Skills quoteColonValues corrupts YAML frontmatter with block scalar continuations
description:
## Location
`internal/skills/skills.go:271-298` — `quoteColonValues()` function

## What's wrong
The `quoteColonValues` function processes the raw frontmatter string line-by-line without understanding YAML structure. It finds every colon in a line and wraps the remainder in quotes if the value contains additional colons. However, it does not account for YAML block scalars (folded `>` or literal `|` style) where continuation lines are part of a multi-line value, not new key-value entries.

For example, a SKILL.md frontmatter like:
```yaml
description: >
  A tool for handling things like
  https://example.com:8080/path
```
The continuation line `https://example.com:8080/path` contains colons. The function wraps it in quotes, breaking the YAML block scalar structure and producing invalid YAML that silently fails skill parsing.

The function also has no test coverage for this scenario.

## Why it matters
Users cannot write skills whose descriptions or compatibility fields contain URLs in multi-line frontmatter values. The skill fails to parse with a confusing YAML error, and the auto-recovery path makes the root cause opaque.

## Suggested approach
Replace the line-by-line approach with a YAML-aware walk that only applies auto-quoting to actual key-value pairs at the top level, not to continuation lines of block scalars. Alternatively, skip lines that are continuations of `>` or `|` prefixed values by tracking whether we are currently inside a block scalar. Add unit tests covering folded and literal block scalars, regular values with colons, and metadata sections.

title: Legacy TUI uses context.Background() for provider config I/O
description:
## Location
`internal/tui/inline_providers.go:239` — `providerCfg()` method

## What's wrong
The legacy TUI's `providerCfg()` method calls `providers.NewManage(nil).Effective(context.Background())` directly:

```go
func (c *inlineChat) providerCfg() config.Config {
    cfg, _, _ := providers.NewManage(nil).Effective(context.Background())
    return cfg
}
```

`Effective()` reads auth state from `~/.config/tau/auth.yaml` — file I/O — but uses `context.Background()`, which has no timeout or cancellation. The TUI has a proper context available (`c.ctx`) but it's not used here.

The comment on this function acknowledges the issue:
```go
// providerCfg re-resolves provider config. inlineChat (the legacy TUI) has no
// request-scoped context to thread through, so this uses Background directly.
```

## Why it matters
If the auth state file read blocks (unlikely but possible on network filesystems), it blocks the TUI goroutine that called it with no way to cancel or timeout. This is inconsistent with how the rest of the codebase handles I/O — proper contexts with deadlines are used elsewhere.

## Suggested approach
Thread `c.ctx` through to `providers.Effective`, or create a short-lived context with a reasonable timeout. The Bubbletea v2 TUI doesn't have this issue since it uses a different code path.
